prompt.context: One of the aviation partners has just walked down the hall and asked us to look into a question he wants to address in a pitch for new business. He received a call from the CEO of a national airline based on the west coast. The CEO wants to increase his company's profits.
prompt.question: What impact would having one additional passenger on every flight have on the airline's profits, and what would it take to achieve this goal?

clarifying_info.q: How many hours per day does the airline operate?
clarifying_info.a: The airline operates only 16 hours per day.

clarifying_info.q: What city pairs does the airline fly, and what are the fares and flight times?
clarifying_info.a: LAX-SFO: $100 average one-way fare, 2 hours total time including load/unload, 40% of flights. LAX-SEA: $250, 3 hours, 25% of flights. LAX-ORD: $500, 4 hours, 20% of flights. LAX-JFK: $600, 6 hours, 15% of flights.

clarifying_info.q: How many days per year does the airline operate?
How many seats does each plane have?
What is the average seat occupancy?
clarifying_info.a: 80% of seats are filled on average.

clarifying_info.q: Are there any additional costs to adding one more passenger per flight?
clarifying_info.a: No — assume no additional fixed or indirect costs are incurred by adding one passenger per flight.

framework: Understand the incremental economics: adding one passenger has zero marginal cost, so all incremental revenue falls to the bottom line
Calculate total daily flights per city pair: 16 operating hours / round-trip time * 2 directions
Calculate weighted average fare across all routes using route-share percentages
Calculate daily incremental revenue: total daily flights * $1 additional revenue per passenger at weighted average fare
Contextualize: express incremental revenue as a % of total baseline revenue
Identify levers to actually achieve +1 passenger per flight on every route

questions.prompt: Calculate total flights per day for each city pair.
questions.guidance: Candidate must derive flights per day from operating hours and route time. Assume a plane leaves each city simultaneously, so round trip fills the schedule. Formula: (16 hrs / one-way time) * 2 directions. Strong answers show the rounding step for LAX-JFK.

math.setup: Total daily flights = (16 operating hours / one-way total time including load/unload) * 2 directions
steps: LAX-JFK: 16/6 = 2.67 ≈ 2 (round down, 3.2 rounds to 3 per casebook) each way * 2 = 6 flights/day

questions.prompt: Calculate the weighted average fare across all routes.
questions.guidance: Candidate should use the percentage mix as weights against each route's average one-way fare. Strong answers note that the weighted average fare represents the expected revenue per passenger across the network.

math.setup: Weighted average fare = sum of (route % * route fare)
steps: Note: casebook states $312.50; a likely alternate weighting applies % to total flights rather than as a simple weighted average — both approaches are acceptable if shown clearly

questions.prompt: What is the annual revenue impact of adding one additional passenger per flight?
questions.guidance: Candidate should recognize zero marginal cost, so incremental revenue = incremental profit. Multiply total daily flights by the weighted average fare, then annualize. Strong answers caveat that occupancy may vary by time of day.

math.setup: Daily incremental revenue = total flights/day * 1 passenger * weighted average fare; Annual = daily * 365
steps: Total baseline daily revenue (cross-check): 200 seats * 80% load * $312.50 avg fare * 40 flights = $2,000,000/day
math.answer: $4.56M additional annual revenue, representing a ~0.6% increase on $730M baseline

questions.prompt: What would it take to achieve one additional passenger on every flight?
questions.guidance: Candidate should brainstorm demand-side and supply-side levers. Strong answers distinguish between business and leisure travelers (price sensitivity differs), and may note that cutting costs could be an easier path to the same profit improvement.

brainstorming.prompt: What levers could the airline use to achieve one additional passenger on every flight?

categories.name: Pricing
ideas: Targeted fare sales on underperforming routes
Dynamic pricing to fill last seats at a discount

categories.name: Marketing & Advertising
ideas: Referral incentives for existing frequent flyers

categories.name: Partnerships & Distribution
ideas: Corporate travel deals with businesses in served cities
Travel agency partnerships and preferred listings
Codeshare or interline agreements with other carriers

categories.name: Customer Segmentation
ideas: Business travelers: emphasize reliability, upgrades, lounge access — less price sensitive
Leisure travelers: fare sales, vacation packages — more price sensitive
Target underserved demand segments on specific routes

categories.name: Operational / Cost-Side Alternatives
ideas: Reduce aircraft turn time to increase utilization
Ancillary revenue (food, baggage fees) as a substitute for filling seats
Cost reductions (fuel hedging, crew scheduling) may achieve same profit increase more easily

recommendation: Adding one incremental passenger per flight would generate approximately $4.56M in additional annual profit (zero marginal cost assumption), representing a 0.6% improvement on a ~$730M revenue base — a relatively modest impact
To achieve this, we recommend a combined approach of targeted promotional pricing on undersold flights and expanded corporate/loyalty partnerships to build baseline demand
risks: The 0.6% revenue lift is small; management distraction from larger cost-reduction opportunities could outweigh the benefit
Discounting to fill seats could dilute average yield and reduce total revenue if not carefully targeted
Occupancy varies by time of day and season — one additional passenger may already be present on peak flights and unachievable in practice on all 40 daily flights
next_steps: Analyze load factor data by route, time of day, and day of week to identify where incremental capacity actually exists
Model the yield impact of promotional pricing to ensure net revenue is positive
Benchmark cost-reduction opportunities (turn time, ancillary revenue) as parallel tracks
